title: EZEKIEL DESCRIBED JERUSALEM AS AN ABANDONED BABY—THEN AS AN UNFAITHFUL WIFE
paragraphs: EZEKIEL DESCRIBED JERUSALEM AS AN ABANDONED BABY—THEN AS AN UNFAITHFUL WIFE

She was thrown away, covered in blood, and left to die. God walked past her and said one word that changed everything: “LIVE.” Then the child He rescued grew beautiful... and eventually used His gifts to betray Him. But the most shocking part of Ezekiel 16 is not Jerusalem’s scandal. It is what God says after He exposes it.
There are chapters in the Bible that comfort you.
There are chapters that encourage you.
And then there are chapters that seem to grab you by the shoulders, turn your face toward the mirror, and refuse to let you look away.
Ezekiel 16 is one of those chapters.
Yet underneath its disturbing imagery lies one of Scripture’s most devastating portraits of human sin—and one of its most astonishing pictures of covenant mercy.
Because Ezekiel 16 is not merely the story of a wicked city.
It is the story of what happens when people forget who found them.
And perhaps that is why this chapter still hurts.
Because some of us have forgotten too.
“Son of man, cause Jerusalem to know her abominations.”

God is speaking about Jerusalem through an extended allegory. The city becomes a woman whose entire life is placed before us—from unwanted infant, to rescued child, to beloved bride, to unfaithful wife, to disgraced sinner, and finally to the astonishing possibility of covenant restoration.
And it begins in a field.
Her umbilical cord has not been properly cut.
She has not been salted according to the customs described in the passage.
Ezekiel says she was thrown into the open field because she was despised on the day she was born.
No mother running toward the crying child.
No human voice saying, “I want you.”
The Hebrew of Ezekiel 16:6 is unforgettable:
“I passed by you and saw you wallowing in your blood.”
Then come the words that change the entire story:
Before she possessed beauty, status, influence, wealth, reputation, or anything she could offer—
Because we have become very skilled at presenting the cleaned-up version of ourselves.
We know what photograph to upload.
We know what testimony to tell.
We know which parts of our history are safe enough to reveal.
We know how to say “God is good” while hiding the room inside our heart that we are terrified to let Him enter.
But God did not meet Jerusalem after she cleaned the blood away.
And maybe somebody reading this needs to understand what grace actually means.
Grace is not God discovering that you were secretly worthy all along.
Grace is God showing mercy to the undeserving.
The Gospel does not begin with humanity climbing toward God.
It begins with God coming toward sinners.
That truth eventually reaches its blazing center in Jesus Christ.
“For while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).
But Ezekiel 16 does not end in the field.
God describes entering covenant with her.
“I entered into a covenant with you.”
This is not merely romantic imagery. The chapter is describing Jerusalem’s relationship to the LORD in covenant terms.
Raises her from abandonment into splendor.
The child nobody wanted becomes like royalty.
And then comes one of the most important sentences in the chapter.
God tells Jerusalem that her beauty became perfect because of His splendor that He had placed upon her.
Everything she became rested upon what God had given.
She began trusting the gift instead of the Giver.
The woman who once possessed nothing began behaving as though everything had always belonged to her.
And suddenly Ezekiel 16 stops feeling ancient.
God gives someone intelligence, and eventually intelligence becomes the reason they believe they no longer need God.
God gives someone success, and success quietly becomes their identity.
God gives someone a relationship, and that person becomes more important than obedience.
God gives money, and money becomes security.
God gives influence, and applause becomes oxygen.
God gives beauty, and the mirror becomes an altar.
God gives ministry, and eventually the ministry itself can become an idol.
Even spiritual gifts can become dangerous when we begin loving what God placed in our hands more than the God whose hands gave it.
Jerusalem took what God had given and used it in idolatry.
The chapter deliberately uses the language of marital unfaithfulness to expose covenant betrayal.
Jerusalem sacrifices her children to idols.
“You did not remember the days of your youth.”
That may be one of the most dangerous spiritual conditions imaginable.
Forgetting what the pit felt like.
Forgetting the prayer you prayed when nobody else could help you.
Forgetting how desperately you once needed mercy.
Forgetting the addiction Christ began breaking.
Forgetting the night you cried until there were no tears left.
Forgetting how empty your life was when sin promised everything and delivered chains.
Forgetting what it was like before grace found you.
And eventually forgetting the One who found you.
Some people do not walk away from God because life became terrible.
Sometimes they drift because life became comfortable.
The prayer that once sounded like “Jesus, please save me” quietly becomes “I can handle this.”
The Bible stays closed a little longer.
Secret compromises begin receiving respectable names.
the rescued heart begins trusting its own beauty.
That is why Ezekiel's language is so severe.
God refuses to flatter Jerusalem while she is destroying herself.
Biblical love does not pretend rebellion is harmless.
Grace never requires God to lie about sin.
Repentance is not God humiliating you for entertainment.
It is the mercy of God calling you away from the thing that is killing you.
Ezekiel exposes Jerusalem's idolatry, injustice, pride, bloodshed, covenant breaking, and spiritual adultery.
And then he makes an observation many readers overlook.
When Jerusalem is compared with Sodom, Ezekiel 16:49 identifies among Sodom's sins pride, abundance, complacent ease, and failure to strengthen the poor and needy.
God notices what we do with abundance.
God notices the person everyone else ignores.
God notices when religious people possess enough to help but train themselves not to see suffering.
Yet even after everything Jerusalem has done, Ezekiel 16 takes another breathtaking turn.
God does not erase the moral seriousness of what happened.
And in Ezekiel 16:60 He speaks of establishing an everlasting covenant.
Then the final verse reaches a word that Christians should recognize as extraordinarily significant.
The expression comes from the Hebrew root כפר — k-p-r, associated with making atonement.
The chapter closes with God speaking of making atonement for what Jerusalem has done.
That does not mean sin never mattered.
It means mercy has not spoken its final word yet.
And for Christians reading the whole biblical story, our eyes are drawn toward Jesus.
Toward the One who did not merely tell dying sinners to rescue themselves, but gave Himself for them.
At the cross, God's holiness is not discarded so that grace can exist.
Sin is taken with terrible seriousness.
Redemption comes at a cost we could never pay.
And resurrection announces that death does not get the final sentence.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally a self-improvement program.
You do not need Jesus merely to make a reasonably decent person slightly nicer.
Perhaps the hardest question in Ezekiel 16, then, is not:
“How could Jerusalem betray God after everything He did?”
Where have I done the same thing?
What gift have you begun loving more than the Giver?
What secret compromise have you renamed so you no longer have to call it sin?
What did Jesus rescue you from that you are slowly walking back toward?
What prayer did you stop praying because life became comfortable?
What conviction have you been silencing?
What part of yourself are you hiding behind Christian language?
Because the God who saw Jerusalem bleeding in the field is not intimidated by what He sees when He looks into the places you hide.
You cannot shock an omniscient God with a confession.
The question is whether you will keep running—or finally come into the light.
Maybe you have fallen farther than you ever imagined.
Maybe you once worshiped passionately, but now your heart feels numb.
Maybe you know Scripture but secretly feel miles from God.
Maybe your browser history and your Sunday worship tell two different stories.
Maybe bitterness has been living inside you so long that you have started calling it discernment.
Maybe pride learned how to quote Bible verses.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong, but spiritually you are exhausted.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something you have never told anyone.
There is no sin so small that you do not need His grace, and no repentant sinner needs to conclude that Christ's mercy is too small for them.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward Jesus.
And think of one person who needs Ezekiel 16 today.
The brother who thinks his past disqualifies him.
The believer who has become comfortable.
The person who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending to have perfect lives.
Sometimes sharing the Gospel begins with one ordinary click that places truth in front of someone you may never have known was struggling.
Not because you need another saved post.
A night when shame tells you to run from God.
A night when temptation whispers that nothing has changed.
A night when success tempts you to believe you no longer need Him.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, understand difficult passages, confront sin honestly, and keep your eyes on Jesus, stay close to this ministry.

Scripture teaches that Christian giving should come from a willing heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Your local church and your own biblical convictions about tithes, offerings, generosity, and stewardship should be honored.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help tremendously.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Help put the truth of Jesus in front of one more wounded person.
Because Ezekiel 16 begins with a baby nobody wanted...
but it does not end with abandonment.
but it does not end with death.
It travels through beauty, pride, betrayal, idolatry, exposure, judgment, shame, remembrance, covenant, and atonement.
And that is why this chapter is so difficult to forget.
The deepest scandal is not merely that Jerusalem became unfaithful.
The wonder is that after exposing the betrayal, God was still speaking about covenant and atonement.
And the Gospel takes us farther still—to Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, calling sinners to repentance and offering forgiveness to everyone who comes to Him in faith.
Maybe you came to this article thinking about ancient Jerusalem.
Maybe God used it to make you think about yourself.
And when shame whispers, “Look what you have done,” look toward Christ and remember what He has done.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when your life has been surrendered to Jesus Christ.
